books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

stimulus.text: In August 1801, the Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone hosted a communion service at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, that became the largest camp meeting of the Great Revival in the West. For six days, from August 6 to 12, crowds estimated at ten to twenty thousand people gathered on the grounds, far more than the log meetinghouse, which seated about four hundred, could hold. Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers all preached, and hundreds took communion at tables set up in the woods.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Disciples of Christ Historical Society account of the Cane Ridge Revival and the National Park Service nomination for Cane Ridge: August 6-12, 1801; Barton W. Stone; estimates of ten to twenty thousand; meetinghouse capacity about four hundred; Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Disciples Historical Society / NPS account of Cane Ridge (1801)
stem: The presence of Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers at Cane Ridge best illustrates which of the following?

options.text: The three denominations had merged into a single church by 1801
options.misconception: Preachers of three churches shared one meeting, so it is easy to read that as a merger.

options.text: Frontier revivals were led only by ministers with university degrees
options.misconception: Ministers led the meeting, so it can look like only educated clergy preached.

options.text: Early western revivals crossed denominational lines and shared preachers and crowds
Baptists and Methodists had driven Presbyterians out of Kentucky by 1801
options.misconception: Methodists and Baptists grew fast on the frontier, so they can look like they pushed Presbyterians out.

rationales.A: The churches stayed separate; they shared a meeting, not a merger. Stone himself later broke with the Presbyterians, but no union happened.
rationales.B: Methodist circuit riders were famously uneducated by university standards, and they preached at Cane Ridge too. Degrees were not the ticket in.
rationales.C: Stone invited Methodist and Baptist preachers to his Presbyterian communion service, and the crowd listened to all of them. The revival crossed lines.
rationales.D: Stone was the Presbyterian host, and Presbyterians were very much present. Nobody was driven out; the meeting was a shared one.
rationales.general:
1. List who preached: a Presbyterian host, plus Methodist and Baptist preachers.
2. Ask what they shared: one meeting, one crowd, and one communion service.
3. Name the pattern: the early western revival crossed denominational lines instead of respecting them.
Background: Stone promoted the meeting as a united sacrament, open to more than his own church.
Remember: when rival churches share a pulpit, the revival matters more than the label.
